newsitem.title: USA: EU meat negotiator heads home, blasts U.S. action.
newsitem.headline: EU meat negotiator heads home, blasts U.S. action.

text.p: The senior Euopean Union negotiator in recently failed bilateral meat inspection talks sharply criticized U.S. moves to curtail meat imports from Europe before heading back to Brussels later today.

Briefing reporters on Wednesday, one day after Washington and Brussels took separate actions that will halt meat and poultry trade between the two sides, Lars Hoelgaard said that despite the stand-off, he hopes talks can be restarted soon.

He said he would be contacting Agriculture Department officials before he returns to Europe later today and may be discussing dates to meet again, but that so far no further negotiations had been scheduled.
Hoelgaard stressed, however, that the U.S. move to require European meat and poultry packing plants to meet U.S. requirements was "totally unjustified" and will only make future talks more difficult.
"This will not impress us," said Hoelgaard. "We're not going to just sit back and let the U.S. take these kinds of actions."
Hoelgaard would not comment on what the EU's next move may be, but said taking the issue to the World Trade Organization is "certainly a possibility."

The EU official denied charges by Washington that Europe's real agenda in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks was to keep U.S. products out of Europe. "We're here to protect our health standards, not protect our trade," he said.
"We have been negotiating in good faith ... We have bent over backwards to accomodate the United States," Hoelgaard said.

Hoelgaard said that he felt significant progress had been made in the last round of talks, and that only a few issues remain unresolved -- specifically the issues of poultry decontamination and chilling, and "some red meat matters."

Washington has long complained that although the United States recognizes equivalent meat inspection systems in Europe and has allowed European meat imports, Europe has insisted that U.S. plants conform to EU standards and has not been practicing equivalency.
The U.S. meat and poultry industry had urged tough action if no agreement was reached in the talks, and industry officials wide applauded Washington's move on Tuesday.
Hoelgaard maintained that equivalency does not mean just agreeing on end-product specifications, but agreeing on specific steps to acheive the final result.

Hoelgaard also said the U.S. action was "totally out of proportion." He noted that new EU regulations on poultry and dairy imports will impact some $75 million worth of U.S. shipments, but that USDA's new rules will halt around $300 million worth of EU products.
